name: quickjs-jit (Longbridge JIT-enabled QuickJS-NG distribution)
baseline: QuickJS-NG interpreter (same revision with the JIT detached); Bun 1.4.0 (JavaScriptCore) listed as the external target
workload: 35 JavaScript micro and mid-size scenarios (scalar loops, fibonacci, property access, typed arrays, collections, JSON, regexp, exceptions) run in 30 retained processes per workload with a paired bootstrap harness.
claimed_speedup: 18.3x-49.2x faster than same-version QuickJS on numeric scenarios (scalar-control-flow 49.2x, quickjs-bitops 42.6x, fibonacci-recursive 27.1x, quickjs-int-arith 18.3x); about 1.0x on collections, JSON, strings, regexp and exceptions; 23 of 35 scenarios faster, 5 slower, 7 tied. Slower than Bun 1.4.0 in all 35 scenarios (0.012x-0.73x of Bun speed).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.98.1 / LLVM 22.1.8, release build; Bun 1.4.0 default flags; QuickJS-NG commit fd0a0210b7be00957751871e7e01b8291268fc29
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i7-13700KF, Linux 7.2.5 x86_64, CPU 8 pinned, powersave governor (an Apple M3 arm64 matrix is also in the README)
stars_or_usage: 15 stars; crate quickjs-jit on crates.io (110 downloads)
tradeoffs: Experimental tiered JIT (baseline plus profitability-driven tier 2) layered on the QuickJS-NG C engine and its Rust bindings; the JIT runtime crate must match the distribution crate patch version exactly (JIT ABI check at startup); native code on x86-64 Linux and arm64; C++ users would need to embed through the Rust crate or the underlying QuickJS-NG C API.
caveats: First-party harness, but raw process records, hashes and machine-readable comparisons are checked in. The baseline is the interpreter of the same engine, not V8: every scenario is slower than Bun (JavaScriptCore), so it does not beat a production JIT. Gains are confined to numeric and scalar code; collections, JSON, strings, regexp and exceptions are unchanged or slightly slower than the interpreter. A previous release regressed real gpui-shell renders (fixed in the measured revision). Very new, 0.12.x.

name: Apogee (Lua 5.5 VM in pure Go with amd64/arm64 JIT)
baseline: C Lua 5.5 (reference interpreter); LuaJIT 2.1 also measured and is faster than Apogee
workload: 17 standard benchmarks (14 Are We Fast Yet programs plus binary-trees, fannkuch-redux and spectral-norm), median of -count 6 runs, each reported as time divided by C Lua 5.5 time; also an 11-workload embedded-Lua suite compared against native Go.
claimed_speedup: With the JIT, 0.57x the time of C Lua 5.5 on the geometric mean of the 17 standard benchmarks (about 1.75x faster, derived from page data), faster on all 17 (Mandelbrot 0.20x, spectral-norm 0.33x, fannkuch-redux 0.49x, DeltaBlue 0.90x); 0.75x on Apple M1 Pro against Lua 5.4; without the JIT 1.8x slower than C Lua. The same table shows LuaJIT at 0.18x, so LuaJIT is about 3x faster than Apogee's JIT (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.1, -count 6, -ldflags=-funcalign=64, taskset to six cores of one CCD; Lua 5.5.1 and LuaJIT 2.1.1788460057 from Arch Linux packages
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9900X3D (amd64, linux); Apple M1 Pro (arm64, macOS) for the second table
tradeoffs: Pure Go (no cgo), so it is not usable directly from C++; JIT only on linux and darwin for amd64 and arm64, other platforms (Windows included) fall back to the interpreter; closures created in a loop and string-heavy code gain little; targets Lua 5.5 semantics.
caveats: Not faster than LuaJIT, the named baseline: its own table puts LuaJIT about 3x ahead. The win is over PUC C Lua, which is the weaker incumbent. The C Lua and LuaJIT rows were measured two days earlier at a different commit than the Apogee rows, and the README says rows move up to 10% between days. About one month old (first commits 2026-09-26), several commits co-authored by an AI assistant, 0 stars. Found under its earlier repository name matjam/luart (GitHub redirected).

name: Cranelift code generator (Bytecode Alliance Wasmtime)
baseline: V8 (TurboFan) for generated-code speed; WAVM (LLVM-based Wasm engine) for compile speed
workload: WebAssembly programs compiled and run through Wasmtime with Cranelift against V8 and the LLVM-based WAVM engine (Figure 22 of a cited paper, per the Cranelift README).
claimed_speedup: Compilation speed approximately an order of magnitude faster than WAVM (LLVM); generated code about 2% slower than V8 (TurboFan) and about 14% slower than WAVM (LLVM).
stars_or_usage: 18.7k stars (wasmtime repository); crate cranelift-codegen has about 51.6M downloads on crates.io; used in production inside Wasmtime
tradeoffs: Code generator tuned for fast compilation with a small trusted code base and fuzzing against V8; backends for x86-64, aarch64, s390x and riscv64. Cranelift itself is a Rust library; C and C++ programs reach it through the Wasmtime C API (wasmtime.h, wasm.h) or by compiling Wasm to native code, not through a stable Cranelift C API.
caveats: Numbers are quoted in the README from a paper (arXiv 2011.13127, cited there); the paper could not be opened here (arXiv blocked), so tier is capped at C until the figure is checked. The runtime result is a loss to V8 (about 2% slower) and to LLVM (about 14% slower); the win is compile speed against LLVM. Figures date from the paper, not the current release. rustc_codegen_cranelift is already catalogued separately.

name: stryke (strykelang): Perl 5 compatible interpreter with bytecode VM and Cranelift JIT
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1.1774896198 (also perl 5.42.2, Python 3.14.4, Ruby 4.0.2, Julia 1.12.6, Raku)
workload: Eight small scripts (startup, fib, loop, string, hash, array, regex, map_grep) timed end to end with hyperfine, mean of at least 10 runs with 3 warmups, process startup included.
claimed_speedup: Beats LuaJIT on 3 of 8: loop 0.74x, array 0.17x, regex 0.07x of LuaJIT time; near parity on string (1.21x) and fib (1.43x); loses on startup (2.20x), hash (3.40x) and map_grep (4.21x). Faster than perl 5.42.2 on all 8 (fib 27x, loop 29x) and than Python 3.14.4 on all 8 (loop 60x, regex 21x). The README ranks it second fastest dynamic language runtime behind LuaJIT.
compiler_and_flags: Cargo release profile opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, panic abort (from Cargo.toml); rustc version not stated
stars_or_usage: 5 stars; crate strykelang on crates.io (4454 downloads)
tradeoffs: Runs Perl 5 source (a superset with parallel primitives), so it is a Perl runtime rather than a Lua or general JIT; Rust crate, no C API seen; JIT can be switched off with STRYKE_NO_JIT=1.
caveats: First-party numbers read from the crates.io README (version 0.17.59); the harness bench/run_bench_all.sh is public but the compiler version is not stated, so tier C. Workloads finish in 2-14 ms and include process startup, so they mostly measure startup and tiny loops, not steady-state JIT speed. The regex row is not like-for-like (LuaJIT uses Lua patterns, stryke uses PCRE). LuaJIT wins 5 of 8 rows. The LuaJIT comparison is one column in a Perl-centred suite.

name: PPy (Pretty Python compiler with LLVM JIT and AOT backends)
baseline: PyPy 3.11.15 (warm); also Numba 0.67, Codon 0.19.6, Cython 3.3, mypyc, Nuitka and CPython 3.14.5
workload: Collatz longest-chain search below 300000, kernel wall time, ten fresh processes each.
claimed_speedup: ppy run (LLVM JIT with Python integer semantics, overflow guards) 41.7 +/- 1.8 ms versus PyPy 3.11 52.8 +/- 0.5 ms (about 1.27x faster, derived from page data) and CPython 3.14 1068.8 +/- 5.5 ms; ppy build --unsafe 30.8 ms versus Numba 32.5 ms, gcc -O3 41.9 ms.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3 -O3, clang 22.1 -O3 for the C rows; PPy built with ppy build / ppy run (LLVM); PyPy 3.11.15 and Numba 0.67 warm
tradeoffs: Compiles only the statically analysable subset of Python (guards fall back to CPython); LLVM backend needs the llvm extra; first ppy run pays about 640 ms to build into the cache (not in the table); the --unsafe rows drop overflow guards and use 64-bit wrap semantics. Python tool, not callable from C++ except through its C or C++17 source emission.
caveats: Single kernel; machine is described only as 'one machine' (no CPU model), and no PyPy reproduction script was seen in the repository, so the PyPy row is not independently reproducible. The eight-kernel suite in examples/15_algorithms compares against C, not PyPy. Pre-1.0 (0.6.0), 15 stars.

name: regexr (Rust regex engine with x86-64/ARM64 JIT)
baseline: regex crate (Rust); PCRE2 with JIT as the second comparison
workload: Regex matching benchmarks (log parsing, URL extraction, Unicode letters, HTML tags, word boundary, email validation, alternation) reported as speedup relative to the regex crate.
claimed_speedup: regexr-jit 3.91-4.09x on log_parsing versus regex (pcre2-jit 3.57-3.71x), 1.95-1.99x on url_extraction (pcre2-jit 2.10-2.13x), 1.43-1.44x on unicode_letters (pcre2-jit 1.65-1.72x), 1.33-1.43x on html_tags (pcre2-jit 0.80-0.85x), 1.00-1.11x on email_validation, 0.88-1.01x on alternation.
tradeoffs: Adds lookarounds, backreferences and JIT without a C dependency; the non-JIT engine only matches regex crate speed; JIT is disabled on WASM; no C API mentioned; built for LLM tokenizer patterns.
caveats: README table only (a heatmap image carries the rest); hardware, compiler and flags are not stated and no benchmark source file was opened, so tier C. The JIT roughly ties PCRE2 JIT and loses to it on url_extraction and unicode_letters. The baselines are not in this category's baseline list (regex crate, PCRE2 JIT; pcre2 is catalogued separately).

name: Hana Jit (LLVM-backed Python JIT, hanajit)
workload: Numeric kernels compiled through llvmlite: a 5-operation fused NumPy expression, float reductions, polynomial evaluation, dot product, fib(30) recursion and call/dispatch overhead, compared with NumPy and Numba.
claimed_speedup: 3.0x faster than NumPy and 3.7x faster than Numba on a 5-operation fused expression; fib(30) recursion 1.7x vs Numba; call/dispatch overhead about 46 ns (3.6x less than Numba). On plain scalar loops it is about equal to Numba (fp reduction 0.78 ms vs 0.74 ms, poly5 1.04 ms vs 0.96 ms, dot product 0.80 ms vs 0.74 ms); with the evolve() genetic tuner 0.23 ms, 0.22 ms and 0.31 ms against Numba 0.74 ms, 0.96 ms and 0.74 ms.
compiler_and_flags: LLVM via llvmlite; Numba 0.66 and NumPy 2.x as comparison; flags not stated
hardware: single core in a shared CI container (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Alpha Python package (about 3,000 lines) for numeric and array code; unsupported code falls back to the interpreter; also exports standalone x86-64 executables, WebAssembly and GPU kernels; Python-only, not callable from C++.
caveats: The README itself says ratios are the signal and absolute times are noisy (shared CI container, no CPU model); benchmark scripts exist in benchmarks/ (bench_experimental.py, bench_reductions.py, fourway.py) but were not run or read here. Plain scalar loops tie Numba because both use LLVM; the larger wins come from fusion, dispatch overhead and the opt-in evolve() tuner. The baseline is Numba, not PyPy; the README also claims 10-100x over CPython, which is not a named-incumbent comparison.
